new_title: Wall Street closes sharply lower as AI cash burn fears spark tech selloff - as it happened
old_text:
Chainalysis: Hackers using 'never-seen-before laundering patterns'
US blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis has spotted that the hackers behind the Binance theft are using " never-seen-before" patterns to launder the stolen assets and stay ahead of the authorities.
They report that thousands of transactions have taken place in a short period, suggesting the attackers are using automation to obscure the trail of funds.
Rather than simply moving funds onward, they repeatedly circulate them among addresses, often sending funds back to addresses involved earlier in the sequence.
While billions of dollars in crypto under their control were denominated in unfreezable cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum, billions more were held in stablecoins like USDT and USDC that can be frozen. It was only a matter of time before the issuers of those stablecoins would freeze those funds - in coordination with law enforcement and industry partners such as Chainalysis.
Freezing funds takes time. The attacker attempted to stay ahead of that process by quickly moving $500 million of stablecoins into a wallet whose job it was to swap out those freezable assets to non-freezable assets. Over nearly 20 minutes it swapped $325 million in stablecoins into $285 million in ETH. Ten minutes later, the exploiter sent the remaining $175 million in stablecoins to stopover wallets, likely trying to move faster than a blacklist or freeze. But the industry caught up with them more quickly than they expected: by 5:14 pm eastern the freezes started.
Bitcoin is dipping lower - it's now down 1.85% today at $77,374, adding to last night's 3% drop.
That might indicate some nervousness about holding crypto assets...
...except some non-crypto assets are also weaker today. Spot silver, for example, is down 4% and just dropped below the $50/oz level for the first time since November 2025.
The Binance hack shows the perils of accidentally clicking on a rogue link, argues Suzy Pallett, president of international cybersecurity conference Black Hat,
"The Binance incident looks set to become the biggest crypto heist in history, and what's striking is how familiar this playbook is. Billions can vanish because one person clicked the wrong thing, and with cyberattacks like these, it all starts by compromising a person, not a platform.
"The question now is not only who executed this attack, but how money like this gets laundered and cashed out once it's been stolen. It's a complicated process, and if we really want to understand how hackers execute attacks like these, we need to be working closely with the people who hunt these perpetrators down.
"Journalists, law enforcement, and the cybersecurity industry have a wealth of intelligence to offer when it comes to large-scale financial attacks, and with international collaboration between these communities, we can collectively work faster and more efficiently to protect against these common exploits."
[as covered earlier, the hack appears to have been perpetrated through a "compromised DevOps engineer's laptop", though Binance insist it was a more complex attack process than just a single click...]
Alexander Shirtcliff, head of commercial disputes and class actions at legal firmEdwin Coe, suggests Binance customers might need to consider legal action to recover losses:
Although Binance insists it has "publicly committed to cover losses", EdwinCoe suggests "blandishments" from the board of Binance are largely for press consumption.
Shirtcliff says:
Taking the current standard user terms at face value, they contain limits to Binance's liability to customers and I see no commitment on using the Secure Asset Fund. Neither will it be quick. How Binance decides to distribute the funds, to whom and when, the value of Bitcoin being volatile, will create a constellation of additional legal issues for the exchange which it will take time to work through.
"It is very unlikely that voluntarily distributed reserves will be enough and customers will have to seek to compel Binance to make them whole. That will mean litigation. A collective action is sometimes the only way for some in cases like this to seek recourse, pooling resources to make litigation viable for many individual victims."
Shirtcliff also suggests there could be litigation concerning who owns the assets which have been frozen since the hack was discovered.
Binance promises to 'weather this storm' as asset recovery begins
Binance has announced that it has "begun recovering affected assets for users" lost in the heist.
It says it is working with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds.
Binance explains that it will use its own reserves of crypto assets to cover losses where possible, and buy other assets in the market:
Binance has already reserved over $6.34B of company funds to cover this incident. $5B of these funds are already held in the exact token assets that were impacted. We are completing the purchase of the remaining amount by buying token assets through market channels and OTC channels. We are doing this to match the format of the remaining token assets and address any asset shortfalls. This step can take longer because some tokens may have low liquidity and OTC settlement also takes time. We will share more progress as soon as we can.
These figures do not include frozen or protected assets, which remain subject to ongoing recovery and verification. Currently, $3bn has been frozen, with thanks to our industry partners. We are working with partners and law enforcement to recover the frozen assets.We will continue to use company resources to cover confirmed shortfall and will provide further verified updates as recovery efforts progress. Ultimately, all user funds will be verified publicly through our Proof of Reserves.
We will weather this storm. Thank you for the support.

James Broomhall, senior associate at Grosvenor Law, says victims of cybertheft often have to turn to the courts:
"Unlike money held in a UK bank account, which may be protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) up to £120,000 per eligible depositor, cryptoassets generally do not benefit from any equivalent compensation regime."
"As a result, victims of major crypto thefts are often forced to pursue urgent tracing and recovery action through the courts, including Norwich Pharmacal applications to compel exchanges and other third parties to disclose information identifying fraudsters and tracing the movement of stolen assets."
UK financial watchdogs monitoring fallout from Binance heist
Kalyeena Makortoff
The UK's financial watchdogs are now monitoring for any potential fallout from the Binance heist.
A spokesperson for Britain's Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said:
"While Binance wasn't registered with the FCA to provide crypto services in UK, we're aware of the reported incident and engaging with them to understand the impact."
While crypto firms are not regulated in the UK, the BankofEngland and FCA will be keeping an eye on any banks, insurers or fintechs that are exposed to Binance, and how that could ultimately hurt the UK's wider financial system.
The BankofEngland is monitoring the Binance hack, according to a source familiar with the matter. However, it is understood there is no active concerns. The Bank of England declined to comment.
Justas Pukys, senior product manager at Surfshark, a cybersecurity company), reckons Binance customres shuold watch out for a potential second wave of scams targeting them.
That would involce criminals impersonating Binance representatives through fake security alerts and requests to transfer funds into "safe" wallets.
Pukys explains:
"The reported $6.3 billion Binance hack is alarming, but cryptocurrency holders should also be on high alert for a potential second wave of scams. Criminals could exploit the panic surrounding the incident to trick people into handing over their savings.
"Scammers may pose as Binance representatives, sending convincing emails or text messages warning that accounts are at risk or offering to help recover stolen funds. Some could even claim to be from Binance's security team, urging users to transfer their cryptocurrency to a supposedly 'safe' wallet. In reality, following these instructions could mean handing your money directly to criminals.
Reminder: Binance'sRichardTeng reassured customers this morning that "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss."
Binance's breach may show the "industrialisation of state-sponsored crime" is underwya, argues Keystone Law's fraud & financial crime partner SyedRahman:
"The more important number in this hack may not be $6.3 billion. It may well be 20 minutes. The attacks had the advantage of preparation and coordination. Everyone responding had to establish what happened in real time. The challenge for the industry is where collaborative efforts in recovering those losses can ever match the speed of a pre-planned attack without sacrificing safeguards that make financial intervention legitimate.
"In essence, the real concern is not that the blockchain failed. It is that systems trusted to control billions of dollars may have been compromised. The weakest point in institutional crypto custody may no longer be the technology holding the assets, but the people and infrastructure authorised to move them.
"We may be witnessing the industrialisation of state-sponsored crime. If North Korean involvement is confirmed, this is not simply a criminal group exploiting a weakness within an exchange. It is a state-linked operation capable of extracting significant sums from global financial infrastructure in minutes.That demands a very different response from governments."
Elsewhere in the financial world, NatWest has rounded out the Q3 bank earnings season with a bit of a whimper.
Pre-tax profits were up just 1.9% for the July to September period, hitting £2.2bn.
That's despite an 8.9% rise in net interest income to £3.6bn, having been offset by an 81% jump in impairment charges - the sums they use for soured loans - from £153m to £277m.
However, NatWest said that impairment charge increase is a comparative issue, reflecting the one-off release of provisions last year, rather than any change in conditions for its borrowers, which has remained stable.
They've also reported higher operating costs, primarily linked to the integration of wealth management business, Evelyn Partners, which the bank bought earlier this year.
The Binance theft raises 'serious questions' for cryptocurrency exchanges, explains Jake Moore, global cybersecurity advisor at security firm ESET
"It is worrying just how quickly billions of dollars can disappear in a modern-day cyber heist, but it is unbelievable that a single laptop has enough privileged access to enable it. If a single device can authorise enormous cryptocurrency transfers, hackers can simply target systems and people until they find a weak link. And there is always one.
"While blockchain transactions can be traced, recovering stolen cryptocurrency is far more difficult, especially when attackers move funds across multiple wallets and blockchains extremely quickly using simple and well-known evasion tactics. North Korea has become increasingly sophisticated in using cybercrime to generate enormous sums of money, but this raises serious questions as to whether cryptocurrency exchanges are doing enough to protect customer assets and whether security and regulation is keeping up.
"Consumers who choose to keep cryptocurrencies should spread their digital assets across multiple reputable platforms and secure hardware wallets (such as their own USB) to reduce the risk of losing everything in a single attack."
News of the Binance heist could knock confidence in crypto assets, suggests Cristiano Ventricelli, vice president of digital assets at Moody'sRatings
"The incident underscores the heightened cybersecurity risks associated with hot wallets, a component already exposed by the 2025 hack on Bybit cryptocurrency exchange. It also illustrates the risk concentration inherent in large, centralized intermediaries.
Stronger institutional controls can reduce some vulnerabilities, but the scale of assets under custody can amplify the impact of a successful breach.
The broader credit and industry implications will depend on the ultimate losses, affected counterparties, asset recovery, and importantly, whether the incident leads to wider disruption or loss of confidence across the digital-asset ecosystem."
Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was probably conducted by North Korea's TraderTraitor.
Chainalysis co-founder and CEO JonathanLevin wrote on X:
We live in unprecedented times. But DPRK are up to their old tricks. We assess @binance hack for $6.4B was likely done by DPRK group TraderTraitor due to links to previous hack.
Industry partners have already frozen ~$3B and we @chainalysis continue to follow all of the funds.
Ethereum accounts for about $3.79bn. That includes 200,630 ETH and 185 other tokens, among them 1.875 billion USDT, 823 million USDC and 88.5 million RLUSD.
Bitcoin outflows total 18,270 BTC, about $1.47bn.
Tron outflows total 612.7 million USDT and 46.4 million TRX, about $628m.
The XRPLedger lost 233.46 million XRP, about $296m.
Solana outflows total 970,500 SOL, about $96m.
Arbitrum, Optimism and Base combine to about $39m, including 74.6 million ARB taken on Arbitrum. Avalanche outflows total about $28m, and Polygon outflows total about $10m.

Wall Street closes sharply lower as AI cash burn fears spark tech selloff
All three major US stock indexes slumped on Friday, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq suffering the steepest loss.
The tech rout was sparked by disappointing quarterly results from Intel and Amazon released late on Thursday.
Chip stocks veered sharply lower, dragging the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index to a monthly loss.
All three main equity indexes closed lower on the week. The S+P 500 and the Nasdaq logged monthly losses, while the Dow exited October with a gain.
According to preliminary data, the S+P 500 lost 139.30 points, or 1.80%, to end at 7,580.21 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 747.73 points, or 2.84%, to 25,440.68. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 571.98 points, or 1.09%, to 51,770.58.
Third-quarter earnings season has passed the halfway mark, with 299 companies in the S+P 500 having reported. Of those, 82% have beaten consensus expectations, according to LSEG data.
Analysts now expect third-quarter S+P 500 earnings growth of 31.6%, year-on-year, per LSEG.
Oil supermajors Exxon Mobil and Chevron both beat quarterly profit expectations, benefiting from soaring profit margins as a result of energy supply disruptions arising from the US-Israeli war with Iran and Russia's war in Ukraine.
Starbucks dipped after the coffee chain forecast an annual revenue decline due to its divestiture of its Chinese business.
Cryptocurrency-related firms Coinbase, Strategy, and Robinhood fell in the wake of reports that hackers stole $6.3bn from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.
US stocks tumbled on Friday, with the Nasdaq suffering its largest one-day percentage drop since 5 June. It followed disappointing quarterly results from Intel and Amazon, which amplified growing worries surrounding AI-related companies' massive spending on the nascent technology. Cryptocurrency-related firms Coinbase, Strategy , and Robinhood fell in the wake of reports that hackers stole $6.3bn from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.
All three major US stock indexes slumped, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq suffering the steepest loss. According to preliminary data, the S+P 500 lost 139.30 points, or 1.80%, to end at 7,580.21 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 747.73 points, or 2.84%, to 25,440.68. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 571.98 points, or 1.09%, to 51,770.58.
Experts identified North Korea as the likely culprit behind the biggest heist in history, and have said the hack was probably carried out by TraderTraitor, an elite north Korean hacking unit. North Korea has a history of crypto hacking, which is estimated to generate half of the country's foreign currency income, generating revenues for its military, including its nuclear weapons programme.
An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance's engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said. The company added later that there had been "additional points of breach" in a sophisticated attack. Binance said it would cover all customer losses as it froze $3bn of the affected assets.
The FBI said it is "aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps". The UK's financial watchdogs are also monitoring for any potential fallout from the heist.

Cryptocurrency-related firms Coinbase, Strategy, and Robinhood fell in the wake of reports that hackers stole $6.3bn from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.
Binance has no cyber insurance and will fund customer reimbursements through company reserves after hackers stole $6.3bn in the world's largest cryptocurrency heist, Reuters is reporting, citing a source close to the exchange.
Binance has said the attack began with a compromised employee laptop and involved multiple breach points. It found no evidence of private-key leakage and said roughly $3bn of affected assets had been frozen.
The exchange holds directors' and officers' (D+O) liability insurance, Reuters's source said, describing crypto cyber insurance as "virtually impossible" for crypto companies to obtain.
The source also said Binance's Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) had no external insurance or reinsurance backing.
D+O cover could respond to claims against executives alleging failings in their oversight, rather than replace stolen assets.
Analysis: How crypto hacking funds isolated North Korea's nuclear programme
Dan Sabbagh
Defence and security editor
North Korea plays by its own rules. The isolated, secretive and autocratic country is largely cut off from the world's economic system - but when it comes to generating foreign earnings it relies on some of the world's most sophisticated hacking.
Experts, such as TRM Labs, quickly attributed the extraordinary $6.3bn Binance cryptocurrency theft to TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit that has also been known as the Lazarus Group. Though the link may not be proven yet, the pattern of behaviour is familiar.
North Korea has a history of cryptocurrency theft dating back to 2017, focusing on the sector's relatively lax security controls as a way of stealing money and generating revenues for its military, including its nuclear weapons programme.
Kim Jong-un, its dictatorial ruler, controls a stockpile of about 50 nuclear warheads, and has been supplying troops and weapons to help Russia in its war in Ukraine. But North Korea is also extremely poor: 40% of the population are undernourished according to the UN and nearly one in five of its children are stunted.
A UN panel of experts, reporting to the security council, said in the spring of 2024 that it was reviewing "58 suspected cyber-attacks" by North Korea "on cryptocurrency-related companies between 2017 and 2023" worth $3bn.
The panel said the cash was estimated to generate half of North Korea's foreign currency income. One unnamed country went further with its estimate: the stolen billions fund "40% of the weapons of mass destruction programmes".
The suspected crypto hacks amounted to as many as 17 in 2023 alone: thefts valued at $750m, and disturbingly, the sums involved are only increasing. The world's largest previous crypto hack took place in February 2025, when $1.5bn was stolen from the Bybit exchange - the work, the FBI said, of TraderTraitor.
Ciaran Martin, a former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, argues that North Korea appears to have targeted crypto because traditional banks have developed sophisticated defences that the fast-growing and lightly regulated sector has yet to match. He said:
Over the last decade, hackers have walked off with nine- or 10-figure sums from crypto hacks on more than 30 occasions. The number of traditional banks who have suffered a loss of more than $100m as a result of a cyber-attack in the same period is zero or one.
The irony is that the internet in North Korea is severely restricted, with access denied to the general population. Maths and science are pushed at school, however, and at university some of the best students are recruited into hacker groups, such as Lazarus, operating under the auspices of the country's Reconnaissance General Bureau spy agency.
The $6.3bn Binance hack could mark an "inflection point" for digital asset insurance buying, with firms needing to look beyond large specie limits and examine the breadth of their protection, Relm CEO Joseph Ziolkowski told Reuters.
Exchanges and custodians had historically prioritised relatively inexpensive specie cover, he said, describing an approach of "form over function". More than $1bn of specie limits was available globally, with less available for cyber cover including digital asset theft.
Ziolkowski described specie as largely protecting private keys. But a malicious intrusion elsewhere in a transaction approval process could enable theft while those keys remained intact.
Binance has said it found no evidence of private-key leakage and identified multiple breach points.
Cyber policies could respond to such intrusions where their wording expressly included digital asset theft, Ziolkowski said. He argued buyers should examine protection across their operations and transaction signing arrangements.
Even holding cyber insurance would not establish that a particular loss was covered, Ed Lewis, global lead for cyber and technology risks at RPC, told the news agency.
"A cyberattack tells you how the trouble started. It does not tell you which policy pays for the missing money," he said.
A precautionary suspension of withdrawals might not satisfy the policy trigger for business interruption cover, Lewis said. Stolen assets, response costs, lost income and customer claims each required analysis against the facts and wording.
Binance has pledged to meet customer losses through its SAFU reserve and company resources, announcing more than $6.34bn of company funds separate from roughly $3bn of frozen assets.
Lewis said frozen assets had not necessarily been returned, while customer reimbursement did not establish that an insurer was paying. "A record theft does not automatically become a record insurance loss," he said.
Tech stocks sell-off deepens, dragging Wall Street toward worst day since June
A sell-off for tech stocks is getting worse Friday on worries that Wall Street's frenzy around AI sent prices too high, the Associated Press reported.
The S+P 500 dropped 1.9% and was on track to erase its gain for October, even though it set its all-time high during the month. The Nasdaq composite was likewise heading toward its worst day since June, as the weakness for technology stocks dragged it down 3.1%, as of 1:20 pm ET. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 511 points, or 1%.
The U.S. stock market remains only 3.1% below its record, which has boosted the value of workers' 401(k) accounts, but the shakiness for stocks in the AI industry is coming just days before Tuesday's upcoming US elections. Worries about AI in general have already become a general and bipartisan concern for voters, and Donald Trump has historically used the stock market's performance as a measure of his own personal success.
In the cryptocurrency industry, meanwhile, stocks tumbled following a hack of Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell toward $77,000 from more than $86,000 earlier this month, and a US-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean unit was likely behind the attack that impacted more than $6 billion worth of crypto at Binance.
Explainer: How big a deal is the $6.3bn Binance heist?
By Dan Milmo and Kalyeena Makortoff
The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a $6.3bn heist that, according to experts, is likely to be the work of North Korea.
This is not the first time a crypto market has been targeted by hackers, and the rogue state has a track record of this type of theft. Here we answer some key questions about what's happened:
Just how big a deal is this?
It could be the biggest heist of any kind in history, according to Elliptic, a consultancy specialising in crypto-related crime. The incident, which took place late on Thursday, is more than four times bigger than the previous largest crypto hack, the $1.5bn one targeting the Bybit exchange last year. Elliptic says there does not appear to be anything comparable in the pre-crypto era.
How was Binance hacked?
It does not appear that private keys were hacked. Instead, a Binance engineer's laptop was infiltrated, which in turn allowed the attackers to drain "hot" wallets. Binance later added that there were "additional points of breach" in its systems as well as the laptop.
Do we know who did it?
This attack has been attributed to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor, a name assigned to it by the US government. The communist state, short of cash and hamstrung by sanctions, has a strong track record of crypto hacking. TraderTraitor emerged from Lazarus, a group working from North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau, a military intelligence agency.
Stocks have tumbled following the hack on the world's biggest crypto exchange.
The price of bitcoin fell toward $77,000 from more than $86,000 earlier this month, and a US-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean unit was likely behind the attack that impacted more than $6bn worth of crypto at Binance.
Coinbase Global fell 12.7% even though it reported stronger results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Strategy, which says it owns about 4% of the total supply of bitcoin, fell 6%, AP reported.
It also reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, while saying its chief financial officer will resign next week for personal reasons.
In the US, Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) chairman Michael Selig told reporters that "we have the ability to trace all this in the blockchain".
Speaking to CNBC, Selig said it was "very concerning" that there had been "several cyber incidents involving crypto" and the CFTC has regulations in place to prevent this sort of attack.
He added that he wants to see a "federal option" so that people will register with the CFTC.
Hackers have stolen $6.3bn from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in what could be the largest theft ever.
The attack saw more than $6bn of crypto assets taken from Binance's own 'hot wallet', apparently after a laptop belonging to one of Binance's development and operations engineers was compromised.
Binance has committed to cover losses from its company funds, and says it is working with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds.
"aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps".
Chainalysis said the hackers appeared to be using "never-seen-before laundering patterns" to avoid the stolen funds being frozen, by switching stablecoins into non-freezable assets such as ethereum.
Crypto assets have dropped in value since news of the hack broke last night.

The $6.3bn Binance hack could mark an "inflection point" for digital asset insurance buying, with firms needing to look beyond large specie limits and examine the breadth of their protection, Relm CEO Joseph Ziolkowski told Reuters. Exchanges and custodians had historically prioritised relatively inexpensive specie cover, he said, describing an approach of "form over function". More than $1bn of specie limits was available globally, with less available for cyber cover including digital asset theft. Ziolkowski described specie as largely protecting private keys. Explainer: How big a deal is the $6.3bn Binance heist? By Dan Milmo and Kalyeena Makortoff The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a $6.3bn heist that, according to experts, is likely to be the work of North Korea. This is not the first time a crypto market has been targeted by hackers, and the rogue state has a track record of this type of theft. Here we answer some key questions about what's happened: Just how big a deal is this? It could be the biggest heist of any kind in history, according to Elliptic, a consultancy specialising in crypto-related crime. The incident, which took place late on Thursday, is more than four times bigger than the previous largest crypto hack, the $1.5bn one targeting the Bybit exchange last year. Elliptic says there does not appear to be anything comparable in the pre-crypto era. How was Binance hacked? It does not appear that private keys were hacked. Instead, a Binance

laptop was infiltrated, which in turn allowed the attackers to drain "hot" wallets. Binance later added that there were "additional points of breach" in its systems as well as the laptop. Do we know who did it? This attack has been attributed to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor, a name assigned to it by the US government. The communist state, short of cash and hamstrung by sanctions, has a strong track record of crypto hacking. TraderTraitor emerged from Lazarus, a group working from North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau, a military intelligence agency. Chainalysis: Hackers using 'never-seen-before laundering patterns' US blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis has spotted that the hackers behind the Binance theft are using " never-seen-before" patterns to launder the stolen assets and stay ahead of the authorities. They report that thousands of transactions have taken place in a short period, suggesting the attackers are using automation to obscure the trail of funds. Rather than simply moving funds onward, they repeatedly circulate them among addresses, often sending funds back to addresses involved earlier in the sequence. While billions of dollars in crypto under their control were denominated in unfreezable cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum, billions more were held in stablecoins like USDT and USDC that can be frozen. It was only a matter of time before the issuers of those stablecoins would freeze those funds - in coordination with law enforcement and industry partners such as Chainalysis. Freezing funds takes time. The attacker attempted to stay ahead of that process by quickly moving $500 million of stablecoins into a wallet whose job it was to swap out those freezable assets to non-freezable assets. Over nearly 20 minutes it swapped $325 million in stablecoins into $285 million in ETH. Ten minutes later, the exploiter sent the remaining $175 million in stablecoins to stopover wallets, likely trying to move faster than a blacklist or freeze. But the industry caught up with them more quickly than they expected: by 5:14 pm eastern the freezes started. James Broomhall, senior associate at Grosvenor Law, says victims of cybertheft often have to turn to the courts: "Unlike money held in a UK bank account, which may be protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) up to £120,000 per eligible depositor, cryptoassets generally do not benefit from any equivalent compensation regime." "As a result, victims of major crypto thefts are often forced to pursue urgent tracing and recovery action through the courts, including Norwich Pharmacal applications to compel exchanges and other third parties to disclose information identifying fraudsters and tracing the movement of stolen assets."
